analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical companies to fund and report toxicity testing of all PFAS 'forever chemicals'.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the EPA, within 60 days, to order comprehensive toxicity testing on all PFAS — man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, water-repellent clothing, firefighting foam, and many other products, and linked in studies to health problems. Companies that make or process PFAS would have to pay for the testing, hand over all records of alleged harm to health or the environment, and submit all health and safety studies they know of. The EPA would have had to make those studies public within four months.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to PFAS through drinking water, food packaging, and everyday products. The bill would have produced public, independent evidence of what these chemicals do to human health — information that currently exists mostly inside the companies that make the chemicals.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA would be required, within 60 days of enactment, to order comprehensive toxicity testing on all PFAS substances, testing them as a class rather than one chemical at a time.
Every company that manufactures or processes PFAS would have to submit all records of significant adverse reactions allegedly caused by the chemicals and all health and safety studies it is aware of.
The EPA would have to make the submitted health and safety studies available to the public within four months, replacing a system where much of this evidence stays in company files.
Exemptions from testing would be allowed only for a chemical whose identical specific identity has already been tested, closing a loophole for minor chemical tweaks.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and processors — the companies that make PFAS and put them into products — would bear the cost of testing and would have to disclose records of alleged harm. Those costs could be passed to consumers in product prices.

drawbacks.text: Testing every PFAS substance as a class would be a large compliance cost for chemical companies and downstream makers of products like nonstick cookware and weatherproof clothing, and some of that cost would likely reach consumers in prices.

Requiring comprehensive testing on all PFAS, including substances with little apparent use or risk, could divert testing capacity from the most dangerous compounds; the bill does try to limit this by requiring the shortest practical testing period.

Requiring companies to turn over 'all records of significant adverse reactions alleged' could surface unverified claims alongside solid science, which the EPA and the public would have to sort through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is public, independent evidence about a class of chemicals that most Americans carry in their blood and that has been linked to serious health harms — the kind of information companies currently hold privately. The cost is compliance spending by chemical makers and some price pass-through. The main design weakness is breadth: mandatory class-wide testing sweeps in many substances, though the bill's short-timeline and narrow-exemption rules push back on that. On balance this is a straightforward information-forcing bill whose costs fall on the industry that created the chemicals.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, and no one ever brought it to a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Representative Sean Patrick Maloney (D-NY) introduced the PFAS Testing Act of 2021 on July 26, 2021.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and one day later to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change.
No other action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Not a single other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill never built the bipartisan support that might have pushed it forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and processors of PFAS came out ahead: they avoided mandatory, at-their-own-expense toxicity testing and public disclosure of adverse-reaction records and health studies. The public continues without federally required comprehensive PFAS toxicity data, and exposure through drinking water and consumer products goes on unmeasured at the chemical level.

for.name: Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to a subcommittee; never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Chemical manufacturers of PFAS
against.role: PFAS producers and downstream product makers
against.what_they_did: Would have borne mandatory testing and disclosure costs under the bill; the industry generally opposes expanded PFAS regulation and liability, and no member of Congress from either party cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill's sole support was one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers of PFAS ( makers of nonstick coatings, water repellents, and fluoropolymer chemicals)
industries.note: The bill would force these companies to pay for comprehensive toxicity testing on all PFAS and to hand over records of alleged harm and internal health studies for public release. Its death leaves their testing voluntary and their internal evidence out of public view, while people exposed through water and products keep bearing the health risk.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers using PFAS (cookware, apparel, food packaging)
industries.note: They would face compliance costs and public information about the chemicals in their products, but as downstream users rather than direct makers they would have been less directly regulated. Disclosure would inform their customers what is in the products they buy.
